fixes.explanation: Tents come up later, but not in David's words here. Uriah talks about the ark, Israel and Judah dwelling in tents. David says, "Go down to your house and wash your feet."

The text says, "But Uriah slept at the door of the palace with all his master’s servants; he did not go down to his house." The king handed him a free night at home, and he chose the doorway. Somebody told David, too. David asks him about it next.

David told him to go down to his house, but that's not what happened. The text says Uriah "…did not go down to his house." He slept at the palace door with his master's servants. Then David was told, "Uriah did not go home."

No tent for Uriah in this verse. He's in Jerusalem, sleeping "…at the door of the palace with all his master’s servants…" Tents come up when Uriah talks about the ark, Israel and Judah dwelling in tents. Where he lies down is the palace door.

Uriah never says a word about the gift. What he says he can't do is go home: "How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife?" He mentions the ark, Israel and Judah in tents, and Joab's soldiers in the open field, first. That's the reason he gives.
David says, "Stay here one more day, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah stays in Jerusalem that day and the next. That comes right after Uriah's answer about not going home.

It's true, baker. The text has David telling Uriah, "Stay here one more day, and tomorrow I will send you back." Uriah stays in Jerusalem that day and the next. David says it right after Uriah says he won't go home.

False is right. Even after David got him drunk, the text says Uriah went out to lie down on his cot with his master's servants, and he did not go home. Once again he sleeps among the servants. The man stays put.

The letter doesn't promote him. It says, "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." I think this one hurts, friend. It's one of the heaviest lines in the passage.

False is right. The letter says, "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." The order is to withdraw from him, not to stay close beside him.

The text doesn't say that. It says some of David's servants fell, and "…Uriah the Hittite also died." This is a heavy part of the story. Uriah was a man who wouldn't go home while the ark, Israel and Judah were dwelling in tents.

Joab doesn't expect a question about being slow. The question he expects is, "Why did you get so close to the city to fight? Did you not realize they would shoot from atop the wall?" The wall is the whole question.

Joab's instructions are for if the king asks why they got so close to the wall. Then the messenger is to say, "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well." That line comes after the question about Abimelech and the millstone.
Eliam is Bathsheba's father, named when David asks about her. The name Joab gives the messenger is Uriah. He's told to say, "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well."

Abishai, Joab's brother (2 Samuel 10:10), isn't in this passage at all. The name Joab gives the messenger is Uriah: "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well." That's the name that closes Joab's instructions.

That's not the message, baker. What comes back is, "Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one as well as another." There's no blame in it. The messenger is even told to encourage Joab with these words.

David doesn't pull anyone back. He tells Joab, "Strengthen your attack against the city and demolish it." Before that, he says, "Do not let this matter upset you…" That's the message the messenger carries back.
